question: What kinds of old photos, videos, screenshots, or documents do users struggle to retrieve?
observation: Among the 157 qualifying (VAGUE_MEMORY_RETRIEVAL) episodes, the target is an ordinary photo in 142/157 (90.4%), video in 9/157 (5.7%), screenshot in 5/157 (3.2%), and document in 1/157 (0.6%).
interpretation: Vague-memory retrieval in this dataset is almost entirely a casual-photo problem, not a document- or screenshot-retrieval problem.
hypothesis: Users retrieving documents or screenshots from memory may rely on different cues than photo-retrieval users, or may be underrepresented here because they give up or complain less publicly about those item types.
limitation: Target type is inferred from a short complaint, not confirmed by the user; the underlying scenario labels also skew toward OTHER/UNKNOWN (91/157), so this dataset has limited power to say anything about non-photo item types specifically.

question: What information do people actually remember about a photo when they start searching?
observation: Among the 157 qualifying episodes, the most common memory clue present is rough_time (64/157, 40.8%), followed by activity (58/157, 36.9%) and context (46/157, 29.3%); person appears in 20/157 (12.7%) and object in 18/157 (11.5%). Only 4/157 (2.5%) mention a specific place, 5/157 mention visible text, and 17/157 (10.8%) carry no identifiable memory clue.
interpretation: Situational and temporal context -- roughly when something happened, or what was going on -- appears more available to users than literal visual descriptors like place, color, or on-screen text.
hypothesis: Users may be better able to describe the circumstances surrounding a photo than its literal visual content, and a retrieval path that depends on literal descriptors may serve this group worse than one that can use situational context.
limitation: memoryClues is derived from a short public complaint, not a structured recall interview; a clue's absence from the text doesn't prove the user doesn't remember it -- they may simply not have mentioned it.

question: What information have they forgotten by the time they search?
observation: 126/157 (80.3%) qualifying episodes name at least one forgotten item; the single most common is an exact date (23 episodes), followed by various specific-content/visual-detail labels (52 episodes combined across near-duplicate taxonomy labels) and location (12 episodes). 31/157 (19.7%) name no specific forgotten item in the text.
interpretation: Exact timing and precise visual/content specifics look like the first things to fade, while the broader situational memory captured above tends to persist.
hypothesis: If exact date and literal content detail are what's missing, a retrieval path that depends heavily on exact metadata (date) or literal content matching may structurally underserve this group even when situational memory is intact.
limitation: The underlying 'forgotten' taxonomy has real label drift across extraction passes (SPECIFIC_CONTENT, SPECIFIC_PHOTO_CONTENT, PHOTO_CONTENT, VISUAL_CONTENT all describe the same idea) -- the 52-episode 'specific content' figure is a manual grouping of near-duplicates, not a single extracted field.

question: How do users formulate a search when their memory is incomplete?
observation: 34/157 (21.7%) qualifying episodes have a captured search query; 29 of those 34 (85.3%) are 3 words or fewer (e.g. 'truck', 'cabinet', 'passport'). A further 74/157 (47.1%) show a SEARCH action in the journey but the query text itself wasn't captured by extraction. The remaining 49/157 (31.2%) show no search action at all -- they went straight to browsing.
interpretation: Where query text is actually known, formulation leans toward short literal keywords rather than full natural-language descriptions, even though users often have richer situational memory available (see the memory-clue finding above).
hypothesis: Users may default to short keyword search out of habit or interface expectation rather than because situational memory can't be expressed -- if so, a retrieval path that could accept a fuller situational description might capture memory this corpus shows users do have.
limitation: Query text is only confirmed for 34/157 episodes; for the 74 with a search action but no captured text, and the 49 with no search action, we cannot confirm query style at all -- the 85.3% short-keyword figure describes only the smaller, known-query subset, not the full 157.

question: How do users reformulate their search after an initial attempt fails?
observation: 17/157 (10.8%) qualifying episodes are tagged observedFailure=SUCCESS_AFTER_REFORMULATION (changing the query/clue succeeded); 1/157 (0.6%) is tagged REFINEMENT_FAILED (reformulation attempted and still failed). Only 4/157 episodes show an explicit REFORMULATE action recorded in the search journey -- most reformulation is visible only in the before/after outcome, not as a distinct logged step.
interpretation: Reformulation works for a meaningful minority when it's attempted, but it's rarely visible as a distinct, repeated step in these complaints -- most users who reformulate appear to do it once, if at all.
hypothesis: Users may not have an established pattern of iterative query refinement (try, adjust, try again) for photo retrieval the way they might for web search -- if confirmed, a single early refinement nudge could capture much of this 10.8%.
limitation: The search-journey log is reconstructed from a complaint's prose, not an instrumented UI trace, so an unreported reformulation attempt would look identical to one that never happened; this likely undercounts real reformulation behavior.

question: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues the user does provide?
observation: 61/157 (38.9%) qualifying episodes are tagged observedFailure=NO_USEFUL_RESULTS -- the user provided some retrieval clue or action but reported no useful candidates. This is the single largest observed-failure category in the primary population.
interpretation: This is the largest point where something breaks after the user has already provided a clue, but the data only shows the user-facing outcome (no useful results), not which internal step actually failed.
hypothesis: possibleSystemExplanation tags appear on many of these episodes as unverified hypotheses -- indexing (64 taxonomy tags across the primary population), ranking (49), semantic_matching (28), query_interpretation (28), metadata_gap (26) -- any of these could explain the 38.9% figure, but none is confirmed by this evidence; only user interviews or engineering telemetry could distinguish them.
limitation: possibleSystemExplanation is an inferred guess about Google's internals from the outside, grounded in nothing the user can actually observe -- it must never be read as 'Google Photos fails to understand clues X% of the time.' The honest answer to this question is: we see the outcome, not the cause.

question: Are potentially relevant results difficult for the user to evaluate or recognize?
observation: 0/157 qualifying episodes are tagged observedFailure=TARGET_HARD_TO_RECOGNIZE (candidate results existed but the user couldn't confidently identify the right one). A related but distinct pattern, TARGET_HARD_TO_LOCATE (results may exist but are buried or require excessive scanning), appears in 22/157 (14.0%).
interpretation: In this corpus, the dominant surfaced complaint is not finding candidates at all, or having to scan too much to find them -- not failing to recognize a correct result once it was seen.
hypothesis: Insufficient evidence in the current dataset to say result-evaluation/recognition is a meaningful failure mode here; it may genuinely be rare, or users may simply not describe this specific moment in a public complaint even when it happens.
limitation: Zero observed instances of one category is itself a finding to treat cautiously -- public complaints bias toward 'I couldn't find it at all' over the more subtle 'I found candidates but wasn't sure which one,' since the latter is a harder experience to put into words.

question: What workarounds do users fall back on after a search fails (browsing, asking someone, giving up)?
observation: Among the 157 qualifying episodes, 42/157 (26.8%) name an explicit workaround action: 13 MANUAL_SCROLL, 7 TIMELINE_SCROLLING, 5 DATE_FILTERING, 2 explicit GIVE_UP, and single-digit counts for the rest (object search, external search, asking another person, etc.); the remaining 115/157 (73.2%) name none. Separately, taxonomy.observedFailure tags 26/157 (16.6%) ABANDONED_OR_NOT_FOUND and 11/157 (7.0%) SUCCESS_AFTER_BROWSING.
interpretation: Manual scrolling/timeline browsing is the dominant named workaround when one is named at all, and abandonment (giving up, whether explicitly stated or just implied by an unresolved complaint) is more common than any single active workaround.
hypothesis: If browsing/scrolling is the main fallback, a cheap improvement to chronological/visual browsing (not search) could capture real value even without improving search itself.
limitation: The 73.2% 'no logged workaround' figure very likely undercounts real workaround behavior -- it means the complaint's text didn't describe a follow-up action, not that the user took none.

question: At which stage does retrieval most often break down (expressing memory, formulating a query, the system understanding it, relevant results surfacing, evaluating results, or recovering from failure)?
observation: Ranked by frequency among the 157 qualifying episodes (taxonomy.observedFailure): NO_USEFUL_RESULTS 61 (38.9%), ABANDONED_OR_NOT_FOUND 26 (16.6%), TARGET_HARD_TO_LOCATE 22 (14.0%), SUCCESS_AFTER_REFORMULATION 17 (10.8%), NO_FAILURE_REPORTED 12 (7.6%), SUCCESS_AFTER_BROWSING 11 (7.0%), EXPRESSION_DIFFICULTY 5 (3.2%), PRODUCT_LOCATION_CONFUSION 2 (1.3%), REFINEMENT_FAILED 1 (0.6%).
interpretation: The most common observed breakdown is 'provided a clue, got nothing useful back,' not 'couldn't express memory in the first place' -- EXPRESSION_DIFFICULTY is the smallest named category (3.2%), so in this corpus memory expression is rarely the stated bottleneck; getting a useful result back from a provided clue is.
hypothesis: If EXPRESSION_DIFFICULTY is genuinely rare, effort aimed at helping users describe their memory may have less headroom than effort aimed at the retrieval step itself -- though see the limitation on possibleSystemExplanation above before treating 'the retrieval step' as a confirmed, specific target.
limitation: These are observed user-facing outcomes (taxonomy.observedFailure), deliberately not mapped onto Google's internal pipeline stages (query understanding, semantic retrieval, result evaluation, etc.) -- that legacy mapping existed in an earlier pass of this analysis and is kept only as secondary/debug data because it asserted an internal mechanism this dataset cannot actually prove.

question: How do these behaviors differ across scenarios (travel, family, documents, screenshots, etc.)?
observation: Scenario labeling is dominated by OTHER (63/157, 40.1%) and UNKNOWN (28/157, 17.8%) -- together 58.0% of the primary population has no specific scenario. Among labeled scenarios, FAMILY (16), FRIENDS (10), and WORK (10) are the largest. Within FAMILY (n=16), NO_USEFUL_RESULTS is 8/16 (50%); within WORK (n=10), NO_USEFUL_RESULTS is 7/10 (70%); within HOBBY (n=8), SUCCESS_AFTER_BROWSING is 3/8, comparatively more common than in other scenarios.
interpretation: Where a scenario is identifiable, NO_USEFUL_RESULTS looks consistently dominant across FAMILY and WORK specifically, suggesting the pattern isn't limited to one context; HOBBY may lean more toward successful manual browsing, though its N is small.
hypothesis: Candidate behavioral pattern worth testing in interviews: does scenario (family vs. work vs. hobby) change which workaround a user reaches for, independent of the underlying failure mode? HOBBY's browsing-success tilt is the single most interesting signal here, not a confirmed pattern.
limitation: 58.0% OTHER/UNKNOWN scenario coverage severely limits this answer -- most within-scenario counts are small enough (n=8-16) that a single episode shifts the percentage by 6-12 points; none of this should be read as a stable scenario-level pattern without primary research, and none of these groups should be treated as a target segment.
